summary:
We built UNTETHERED, an onboard health monitoring prototype for astronauts who cannot get an immediate response from Earth. Crew members can describe symptoms in their own words and compare their resting heart rate, sleep, and activity with their own past readings. This helps them spot changes that might go unnoticed in a single reading.

Preset rules trigger alerts without waiting for the AI. A small language model runs onboard and explains flagged changes using reference material stored locally. The software checks the numbers and citations before showing an explanation and withholds it if the evidence is missing or the checks fail.

In a simulated Mars mission, we demonstrated how the system can adjust cabin lighting based on sleep records and queue alerts for transmission when contact resumes. This gives astronauts a way to see what changed and what to check first, while preserving a record for the ground medical team.
details:
What it does and how it works

Crew Health is health-monitoring software for crews on long Mars missions. On Mars, messages to Earth take tens of minutes, and during solar conjunction contact is nearly lost for about two weeks. The app changes how much it acts on its own depending on the link to Earth (connected, delayed, blackout).

Delayed: when sleep and heart-rate variability (HRV) drop below the crew member’s own baseline, the habitat adjusts the cabin lighting automatically. A schedule change is applied only after the crew member approves it, and both are released on their own once the next day shows recovery.

Blackout: an urgent symptom such as chest pain raises an alert immediately through rules, without waiting for the AI. Two designated crew members must each give consent before a report is saved. That report is the first thing sent to Earth when contact returns.

Benefits

Instead of handing tired crew members more dashboards and tasks, the habitat changes first. Decisions that are hard to undo stay with people, and every adjustment and explanation links to its source paragraph.

Intended impact

We want crew members not to be left deciding alone when Earth’s medical team cannot reach them. The same approach fits other places with unreliable links, such as Antarctic stations and remote sites.

Tools used

Frontend: React 19, Vite, React Router, Chart.js, Three.js (3D body view)

Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLite

AI: Gemma 4 12B (4-bit), run locally on an Apple Silicon Mac with mlx-lm, with a LoRA adapter we trained during the event. It works without internet.

Evidence: knowledge paragraphs summarized from public sources such as NASA’s Human Research Program

Collaboration: GitHub pull requests with automated review

What makes it creative

The idea is “the farther Earth gets, the more the spacecraft wakes up.” The same app shifts its role with the link: it suggests, then adjusts on its own, then requires two-person consent. Rules make the call, people make the decisions, and the AI only explains.

What the team considered

AI can be wrong, so it is kept out of urgent decisions, and an explanation that fails verification is put on hold.

One person’s consent can never count twice, and a packet that fails to arrive is resent in the next comm window.

The screen states that the data is synthetic, the environment controls are simulated, and the medical paragraphs have not yet had expert review.
